note: Restaurants and Eating Out lesson (board photo), content v3, written at A2 level: 27 words and 1 grammar rule (past continuous). 'Place / make an order' is a collocation of Order (with a Word Partners check).

words.meaning: To eat a meal in a restaurant, not at home.
situations: We eat out every Friday at a small fish restaurant.
gaps: We don't want to cook tonight, so let's ______.
My parents like to ______ on their wedding anniversary.
hints: To have a meal in a restaurant.
Eat + a small word that means 'not inside'.

commonMistakes.sentence: We ate outside at a restaurant last night.
commonMistakes.correction: We ate out at a restaurant last night.
commonMistakes.why: 'Eat out' means eat at a restaurant; 'eat outside' means eat in the open air.

collocationChecks.sentence: I'm too tired to cook. Let's eat ______ tonight.
collocationChecks.explanation: Eat out = have a meal in a restaurant.

words.meaning: To ask for food or drinks in a restaurant (verb); the food or drinks you ask for (noun).
situations: I'd like to order the chicken with rice, please.
gaps: Are you ready to ______, or do you need more time to look at the menu?
Can I ______ a large pizza and two lemonades, please?
hints: What you do when you tell the waiter what you want.
It rhymes with 'border'.

commonMistakes.sentence: Can I do an order, please?
commonMistakes.correction: Can I place an order, please?
commonMistakes.why: We place or make an order — we don't 'do' an order.

collocationChecks.sentence: I'd like to ______ an order for two pizzas, please.

words.meaning: To ask a restaurant to bring food to your home.
situations: It was raining, so we ordered delivery from the burger place.
gaps: It's raining and we're tired — let's ______ from the pizza place tonight.
When you ______, the food comes to your door in about thirty minutes.
hints: The food comes to your home.
Order + the word for bringing things to your door.

commonMistakes.why: We say 'order delivery' without 'a'.

words.meaning: The way waiters and other workers help you in a restaurant or shop.
situations: The service in this café is always fast and friendly.
gaps: The food was good, but the ______ was slow — we waited an hour for our drinks.
This hotel is famous for its friendly customer ______.
hints: How the waiters help you.
It comes from the verb 'serve'.

commonMistakes.why: 'Service' is singular here: the service was.

words.meaning: A style of cooking from a country or area.
situations: I love Italian cuisine, especially pasta and pizza.
gaps: Koshari and molokhia are famous dishes of Egyptian ______.
This restaurant serves Japanese ______, like sushi and noodles.
hints: The type of cooking from one country.
It sounds like 'kwi-ZEEN'.

commonMistakes.why: For a country's style of cooking, say 'cuisine', not 'kitchen'.

words.meaning: A small dish you eat before the main dish.
situations: We had soup as an appetizer and then grilled fish.
gaps: We shared some soup as an ______ before our steaks came.
I'm not very hungry, so I'll just have an ______ and skip the main dish.
hints: The small food at the start of a meal.
It starts with 'app-'.

commonMistakes.correction: As an appetizer, I want soup.
commonMistakes.why: Say 'as an appetizer' or 'for an appetizer' — don't forget 'an'.

words.meaning: The biggest and most important part of a meal.
situations: For my main dish, I had chicken with rice.
gaps: I had soup to start, and for my ______ I had grilled fish with rice.
The steak is the ______; the salad and chips come with it.
hints: The big part of the meal, after the small starter.
Main + another word for a plate of food.

commonMistakes.why: We say 'main dish' (or 'main course').

words.meaning: A small amount of food you eat with the main dish, like chips or salad.
situations: I'll have the burger with a salad as a side dish.
gaps: I'll have the chicken, and rice as a ______, please.
Would you like salad or chips as a ______ with your burger?
hints: Small food that comes next to the main dish.
Side + another word for a plate of food.

commonMistakes.correction: I want chips as a side dish.
commonMistakes.why: Say 'as a side dish' (or 'as a side').

words.meaning: Sweet food you eat at the end of a meal.
situations: For dessert, we had chocolate cake.
gaps: For ______, we had chocolate cake and ice cream.
I'm full, but I always have space for something sweet like ______!
hints: Sweet food at the end of the meal.
Two s's — like 'sweet stuff'.

commonMistakes.why: Dessert (ss) is sweet food; desert (s) is a dry, sandy place.

words.meaning: A large, hot, dry area of land with a lot of sand.
situations: The Sahara is a very big desert.
gaps: Camels can walk for days in the ______ without water.
The Sahara is the biggest hot ______ in the world.
hints: A place with sand and very little rain.
One s — don't confuse it with sweet food.

commonMistakes.sentence: We ate a nice desert after dinner.
commonMistakes.correction: We ate a nice dessert after dinner.
commonMistakes.why: Desert = sand; dessert = sweet food.

words.meaning: Knives, forks and spoons.
situations: Please put the cutlery in the drawer.
gaps: The waiter put clean ______ next to each plate.
Where do you keep the ______? I need something to eat my steak with.
hints: The metal things you eat with.
It starts with 'cut-'.

commonMistakes.why: 'Cutlery' is uncountable — no 'a', no plural.

words.meaning: A tool with points that you use to pick up food.
situations: I eat spaghetti with a fork.
gaps: You eat spaghetti with a ______ — you turn it to catch the noodles.
Push your ______ into a piece of chicken and lift it to your mouth.
hints: You use it to pick up food; it has points.
It rhymes with 'pork'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I eat soup with a fork.
commonMistakes.correction: I eat soup with a spoon.
commonMistakes.why: A fork has points, so we use a spoon for soup.

words.meaning: A tool with a sharp edge for cutting.
situations: Can I have a knife to cut this steak?
gaps: Be careful, the ______ is very sharp.
You need a ______ to cut this steak.
hints: You cut food with it.
The 'k' is silent.

commonMistakes.why: The plural of knife is knives.

words.meaning: A tool with a small round end for eating soup or mixing tea.
situations: She mixed her tea with a spoon.
gaps: You can't eat soup with a fork — take a ______.
Add one ______ of sugar to my tea, please.
hints: You eat soup with it.
It rhymes with 'moon'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I put two spoon of sugar.
commonMistakes.correction: I put two spoons of sugar.
commonMistakes.why: Use the plural: two spoons.

words.meaning: To put plates, glasses and cutlery on the table before a meal.
situations: Can you set the table? Dinner is almost ready.
gaps: Can you ______ for dinner? Put out four plates and four glasses.
The guests are coming at eight, so please ______ before then.
hints: What you do before a meal.
Set + the + the thing you eat on.

commonMistakes.why: We say 'set the table' (or 'lay the table').

words.meaning: To take the plates and glasses away after a meal.
situations: After lunch, I cleared the table and washed the dishes.
gaps: After dinner, the kids ______ and their dad washes the dishes.
Can you help me ______? Put the dirty plates in the kitchen.
hints: What you do after a meal.
The opposite of 'set the table'.

commonMistakes.sentence: Can you clean the table from the plates?
commonMistakes.why: 'Clear the table' = take the dishes away.

words.meaning: To try a little food; to have a flavour (verb). The flavour of food (noun).
situations: Can I taste your soup? It smells good.
gaps: Can I ______ your soup? It smells really good.
This medicine has a horrible ______, like old coffee.
hints: What your tongue tells you about food.
It rhymes with 'paste'.

commonMistakes.why: Taste + adjective (tastes good), or taste like + noun (tastes like chocolate).

words.meaning: Tasting of sugar.
situations: This mango is very sweet.
gaps: This tea is too ______ — you put three spoons of sugar in it!
Children usually love ______ snacks like chocolate and cake.
hints: How sugar tastes.
It rhymes with 'meet'.

commonMistakes.why: The adjective is 'sweet'.

words.meaning: Salty or spicy, not sweet.
situations: I prefer savory snacks, like cheese and crackers.
gaps: I don't like sweet breakfasts; I prefer ______ food like eggs and cheese.
Would you like a ______ pie with meat, or one with apples and sugar?
hints: Food that is not sweet.
It starts with 'sav-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I like savory cakes with chocolate.
commonMistakes.correction: I like sweet cakes with chocolate.
commonMistakes.why: Chocolate cake is sweet; savory food is salty or spicy.

words.meaning: Tasting of salt, or with too much salt.
situations: These chips are very salty.
gaps: The sea water is too ______ to drink.
These chips are very ______ — I need a glass of water.
hints: How sea water tastes.
It comes from 'salt'.

commonMistakes.sentence: The soup has too much salty.
commonMistakes.correction: The soup is too salty. / The soup has too much salt.
commonMistakes.why: 'Salty' is an adjective; 'salt' is the noun.

words.meaning: To make you very hungry because food looks or smells so good.
situations: The smell of grilled chicken makes my mouth water.
gaps: Pictures of pizza can ______ even when I'm not hungry.
The smell from that bakery is enough to ______.
hints: When good food makes you want to eat right now.
Your mouth gets wet.

commonMistakes.sentence: The cake made my mouth to water.
commonMistakes.correction: The cake made my mouth water.
commonMistakes.why: Make + someone + base verb, without 'to'.

words.meaning: To share the cost of a meal so each person pays part of it.
situations: There were four of us, so we split the bill.
gaps: The meal cost 600 pounds, so the three of us decided to ______.
Let's ______ — you pay for your food and I'll pay for mine.
hints: Everyone pays part of the cost.
Split + the + the paper with the price.

commonMistakes.why: We say 'split the bill' (or 'go halves').

collocationChecks.explanation: Split the bill = share the cost.

words.meaning: Used to say that you will pay for someone else's meal or drink.
situations: Put your money away — this is my treat.
gaps: Put your money away — lunch is ______ today.
Don't worry about the bill. This coffee is ______.
hints: You say this when you pay for your friend.
My + a word for something nice you give someone.

commonMistakes.why: We say 'my treat' (or 'it's on me').

words.meaning: I will pay for this.
situations: Don't pay for the drinks — it's on me.
gaps: Don't take out your wallet — ______. You paid last time.
You helped me move house, so dinner tonight — ______!
hints: You say this when you want to pay.
It's on + the person who pays.

commonMistakes.why: After 'on', use the object pronoun: me.

words.meaning: The restaurant gives it to you for free.
situations: The waiter brought us free tea and said, "It's on the house."
gaps: The owner knows my dad, so when we tried to pay for the cake, he smiled and said, "No, no — ______!"
We waited a long time, so the manager gave us free drinks and said, "______."
hints: The restaurant pays, so it's free for you.
'House' here means the restaurant.

commonMistakes.why: The fixed expression uses 'the house'.

words.meaning: To take the biggest part of something.
situations: My friend took the lion's share of the meal.
gaps: My brother always tries to ______ of the pizza — he eats five slices!
The boss's son will ______ of the money, and the workers will get very little.
hints: To take the biggest part.
Think of the king of animals.

commonMistakes.why: Don't forget the 's: the lion's share.

words.meaning: Slowly, in small amounts or steps.
situations: You should eat your meal bit by bit.
gaps: Eat your food slowly and ______, not all at once.
My English is getting better ______.
hints: Slowly, one small part at a time.
The same small word two times, with 'by' in the middle.

commonMistakes.sentence: He learned it bit to bit.
commonMistakes.correction: He learned it bit by bit.
commonMistakes.why: The binomial is fixed: bit by bit.

grammar.explanation: Use the past continuous for an action that was in progress at a time in the past. I / he / she / it + was; you / we / they + were. Negative: wasn't / weren't + verb-ing.

commonMistakes.why: We / you / they + were.
was / were + verb-ing.

questions.prompt: He ______ football at 6 — he was at home with his family.
______ you having dinner at 8 last night?

questions.sentence: We was waiting for our food at nine.
questions.fix: We were waiting for our food at nine.

questions.sentence: She was drinking coffee in the café at ten.
questions.alternative: She was drink coffee in the café at ten.
